analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health service giving free comprehensive health care to everyone in the United States.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a committee markup or floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a government-run United States Health Service giving free, comprehensive health care — doctor visits, dental, vision, mental health, prescriptions, long-term care, and reproductive services — to every person in the country, delivered by salaried government health workers and financed by new taxes on individuals and corporations. It also would have guaranteed workers paid time off for medical care and given health workers union rights. It was referred to three House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person in the United States — including the more than forty million the bill's findings say lacked coverage — would be entitled to free comprehensive care: primary and specialty care, dental, vision, mental health, long-term care, prescription drugs, and reproductive services, regardless of income, health status, or employment [S2] [S3]. Workers would also earn one hour of paid health leave for every 35 hours worked to attend care for themselves or a dependent [S3]. Health workers would gain federal employee protections, union representation through card-check, and loan repayment for serving the Service [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes every person in the United States — regardless of income, employment, health status, or immigration-adjacent status — eligible for free comprehensive care from any Service facility, ending coverage tied to a job [S2] [S3].

Guarantees an enumerated set of patient rights, including a right to appeal any denial or delay of medically necessary care, access to user advocates, and legal assistance to enforce those rights [S3].
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so workers earn one hour of paid health leave per 35 hours worked, usable for their own or a dependent's medical care [S3].
Requires free reproductive services including contraception, abortion, and a full range of childbirth options, with strict informed-consent rules for sterilization [S3].
Targets resources at underserved inner-city, rural, and minority populations and gives Service workers union representation via card check, federal employee protections, and a right to strike [S3].

analysis.who_pays: New percentage surtaxes on individual, estate, trust, and corporate income taxes, plus employer contributions, would fund a new Health Service Trust Fund; the bill also transfers the existing Medicare trust fund assets into it [S2]. Employers would pay higher taxes but would no longer provide or pay for private health benefits [S3].

drawbacks.text: Funding would come from new percentage surtaxes on individuals, estates and trusts, and corporations, on top of redirecting the existing Medicare payroll taxes and trust funds into the new Health Service Trust Fund — a major and hard-to-reverse shift in who pays for care [S2].

Care would be delivered almost entirely through salaried Service facilities, and the bill allows care to be denied or postponed based on limits in available personnel and facilities — the rationing-by-waiting objection a single-system design must answer [S3].

The transition would be disruptive: private insurance jobs would disappear (the bill budgets up to 1 percent of the Service budget for retraining displaced insurance and administrative workers), and students in the new health team schools would be required to work for the Service for at least two years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — free comprehensive care for everyone, including the forty-plus million uninsured the bill cites — was enormous, and the bill included real accountability mechanisms like an Inspector General and patient appeal rights. But the cost side was equally enormous and thinly specified: new surtaxes on individuals and corporations, absorption of the Medicare trust funds, and a forced conversion of the entire delivery system to salaried public facilities within years. Even a well-designed version of this scale would have been the largest domestic restructuring since the 1960s, and this bill received no committee scrutiny to test whether the financing and transition would work. The strongest honest objection is not the goal but the lack of any demonstrated path: the bill died before anyone had to defend or fix its numbers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from September 2003 onward, never got so much as a committee vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on September 4, 2003 with 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1] [S4].

It was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and then to their subcommittees on health, employer-employee relations, and workforce protections [S5].
No committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever appears in the action history; the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance, pharmaceutical, and for-profit hospital industries kept the existing system, with no new taxes or public alternative created; the more than forty million uninsured Americans cited in the bill's findings gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and for-profit health care

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred; all 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded.

industries.note: The bill routes all financing through a single public trust fund and makes the Service the provider of care, ending the private insurance industry's core business; it even budgets retraining money for displaced insurance employees.
Drugs and medical supplies would be purchased and distributed by the Service through a national formulary, replacing the current market where insurers and patients pay negotiated or list prices.

industries.industry: For-profit hospitals and managed care companies
industries.note: Care would be delivered by salaried workers in Service facilities, and the Service could use eminent domain to acquire property for facilities, displacing the for-profit delivery model the bill's findings blame for inflated costs.
Employers would face new corporate surtaxes and lose control of health benefits, but would stop paying private premiums, so the net effect depends on how the taxes compared to current coverage costs.

industries.industry: Physicians and health professionals in private practice
industries.note: Practitioners would be guaranteed hiring preference, federal-employee protections, and loan repayment, but decisionmakers would be barred from any paid private health care work and new graduates would owe years of Service employment.
